paper.citation: Gołaś A, Pietraszewski P, Roczniok R, Terbalyan A, Maszczyk A, Opaliński R, Zając A. Effects of an 8-week pre-season targeted training on sprinting performance, agility and lower limb muscular asymmetries in elite soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(4):69-76.
paper.abstract: Thirty-two elite soccer players were randomly divided into an experimental group and a control group of 16 each for an 8-week pre-season. The experimental group completed speed, agility and unilateral bodyweight strength sessions, while the control group completed circuit training matched for volume and intensity. Pre- and post-season sprint, change-of-direction and surface EMG measures were compared between groups.
paper.tldr: An 8-week pre-season block of speed, agility and unilateral bodyweight strength work improved 5 m sprint, agility and change-of-direction deficit more than a matched circuit-training control in these elite soccer players. Surface EMG asymmetry indices also fell, but injury risk was not measured.
paper.methods: Randomised allocation of 32 elite soccer players to experimental and control groups of 16. Testing included 5 m and 30 m sprints and a ZigZag change-of-direction test timed with photocells, plus surface EMG from quadriceps, hamstrings and gluteal muscles during treadmill running. The experimental group trained speed twice a week, agility three times a week and six unilateral bodyweight exercises four times a week, with an extra set added each week, and a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests was used.
paper.findings: The experimental group improved 5 m (1.064 to 0.98 s), 30 m (4.24 to 4.08 s), agility (6.17 to 5.18 s) and change-of-direction deficit (1.93 to 1.11 s), and after training it outperformed the control group on 5 m, agility and deficit. EMG asymmetry indices for quadriceps (AQ), hamstrings (AH) and glutes (AG) fell in the experimental group, with the largest disproportion reduction reported in the gluteal muscles.
paper.limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. It notes that plyometrics, age, sex and competition level were not examined, and the training was designed to mirror the test conditions, so transfer to match play is not established. Injury risk was not measured, even though the authors discuss asymmetry as an injury-risk factor.
paper.practicalImplications: Pre-season programmes could pair sprint and change-of-direction work with a short, progressive set of unilateral bodyweight exercises such as bird dog, single-leg glute bridge, dead bug, side plank, reverse lunge and clamshell. Staff should not read these results as proof of reduced injury risk, because injuries were not tracked.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use this as a model for pre-season programming that pairs sprint and change-of-direction training with unilateral, movement-pattern strength work. EMG was used here to track muscle activity balance across training, although this was a single-group, single-team study.
paper.rtp: The study included no injured players and did not evaluate return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot be used to guide return to sport or readiness testing.
